title: Fire at work
about: Helps you act in a fire at work: warn others, get out, call 111 and ask for FIRE, and decide whether it is safe to use a fire extinguisher. Based on Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) advice.

sources.name: Fire and Emergency New Zealand, Fire Action Notice
Fire and Emergency New Zealand, Example Evacuation Scheme Document (office building exemplar)
Fire and Emergency New Zealand, Our 3-Step Escape Plan and business fire safety checklist
Fire and Emergency New Zealand, Commercial use of fire extinguishers
Fire and Emergency New Zealand, Fire extinguisher position document
Fire and Emergency New Zealand, Fire extinguishers (home fire safety)

warning: In a fire, get out and stay out. Call 111 and ask for FIRE.
audience: Anyone at work in New Zealand who finds a fire or hears the fire alarm
version: Fire and Emergency New Zealand Fire Action Notice, evacuation scheme exemplar and fire extinguisher pages (no dates shown; site footer © 2026), read 19 Nov 2026

options.label: There's a fire, or the alarm is going
Should I use the fire extinguisher?
Get ready: what to know before a fire

lines.text: Shout "Fire, Fire, Fire" to warn people near you.

quotes.text: WARN OTHER BUILDING OCCUPANTS
Warn occupants in the immediate area by shouting “Fire, Fire, Fire”

lines.text: If the alarm isn't going, set it off at the nearest call point: a red box with a break-glass panel.

quotes.text: Activate the nearest manual call point if the alarm is not already sounding
these are red boxes with break-glass panels

lines.text: Call 111 from a safe phone and ask for FIRE. If you can't safely, call as soon as you are out.

quotes.text: DIAL 111 FROM A SAFE PHONE – ASK FOR FIRE
Call emergency services as soon as you are out and safe.

lines.text: Leave the building now, by the nearest exit.

quotes.text: YOU MUST LEAVE THE BUILDING IMMEDIATELY USING THE NEAREST EXIT

lines.text: Be fast. Don't stop for your things.

quotes.text: Be fast
Don't spend time trying to save possessions.

lines.text: Check the area you're in for other people. Help anyone who needs it on the way out.

quotes.text: Check the area you are in for other people
Evacuate the building, assisting anyone else you see on the way
Assist others to evacuate as required

lines.text: On an upper floor, use the stairs.

quotes.text: Evacuate the building, if on upper floors use the stairs

lines.text: Lifts: FENZ doesn't say. Follow your workplace's plan.
Lifts are a gap (none of the FENZ pages read mention them). The after-hours lines are general actions (not warden duties), so they are used here.
Get low if there is smoke. Smoke is more deadly than flames.

quotes.text: Get low
Smoke is poisonous and more deadly than flames.

lines.text: Close doors behind you. A closed door buys you time.

quotes.text: Close doors
A closed door buys you time.

lines.text: "Get low" and "Close doors" come from FENZ's 3-Step Escape Plan, written for homes but shown on FENZ's business pages. The office example only lists closing doors as a training topic. The provenance is explained in the Get ready route and in Notes, not here.
If 111 hasn't been called yet, call now and ask for FIRE.

quotes.text: Call emergency services as soon as you are out and safe.
Ask for FIRE.

lines.text: Give the address clearly. Say if anyone is still inside or missing.

quotes.text: Clearly state your address and let the operator know it anyone is still inside or has not made it to the safe meeting place.

lines.text: Go to your workplace's assembly point.

quotes.text: ASSEMBLE

lines.text: It should be on the Fire Action Notice on your wall.
The Fire Action Notice leaves the assembly point blank for each building to fill in. The example scheme's grass area and flagpole belong to that made-up building only, so they are not shown.
Don't go back inside for any reason. People have died going back into a fire.

quotes.text: Don't leave the meeting place to go back inside for any reason.
People have died by going back into a fire.

lines.text: Your workplace's plan says who can give the all-clear.

App wording. In FENZ's example scheme the all-clear is given by "the Head Warden or Fire and Emergency" (Area Wardens' duty), but that is the made-up building's set-up, so it isn't quoted as the user's instruction.
You did the right thing by getting out.
First, shout "Fire, Fire, Fire" and set off the fire alarm.

quotes.text: WARN OTHER BUILDING OCCUPANTS
Operate the nearest fire alarm manual call point

lines.text: Only use an extinguisher if it's safe. Life is more important than property.

quotes.text: Only use fire extinguishers when it is safe to do so
Remember, life is more important than property.

lines.text: The fire must be no bigger than a waste paper basket or a pot on a stove, and in a place that is safe to get near.

quotes.text: when the fire is no larger than a waste paper basket or pot on a stove.
It's safe to do so considering the size and location of the fire

ask.question: Is the fire that small, and safe to get near?

lines.text: You need a safe way out, so you can back away from the fire.

quotes.text: Always have a safe path of escape
You can safely access and retreat from the fire.

ask.question: Do you have a safe way out?

lines.text: 111 must have been called, and everyone else must be out.

quotes.text: ensure Fire and Emergency has been called.
Everyone has been evacuated and accounted for at your safe meeting place.

lines.text: "Everyone is out" comes from FENZ's home page; the commercial page only asks for a safe escape path and FENZ called. The stricter rule is kept. Two conditions in one question to keep the route short; both must be yes.

ask.question: Has 111 been called, and is everyone else out?

lines.text: Gas fire: turn off the gas supply first.

quotes.text: Always turn off the supply of gas before extinguishing gas fires.

lines.text: Cooking oil or fat: never use dry powder. Live electricity: don't use wet chemical.

quotes.text: you should never use it on a cooking oil or fat fire
However, don't use wet chemical extinguishers on fires with a live electrical source.

lines.text: Metal fires need a special extinguisher.

quotes.text: Special purpose extinguishers are available for metal fires.

lines.text: FENZ's table of which extinguisher suits which class could not be read, so this screen gives only the pairings FENZ states in words. The question is backed by "confident you understand how to use the extinguisher correctly" (home page). The gap is explained in the Get ready route.

ask.question: Are you sure this extinguisher is right for this fire?

lines.text: Only go ahead if you're confident you know how to use it.

quotes.text: You're confident you understand how to use the extinguisher correctly.

ask.question: Are you confident you know how to use it?

lines.text: It only lasts 10-15 seconds once started.

quotes.text: your extinguisher will only last 10-15 seconds once started

lines.text: Pull the safety pin or remove the clip.

quotes.text: Pull the safety pin or remove the clip.

lines.text: Test squirt it to check it works.

quotes.text: Test squirt the extinguisher to make sure it is working.

lines.text: Aim at the base of the fire from a safe distance (most extinguishers work from about 2-3 metres).

quotes.text: Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire from a safe distance.
Most extinguishers are designed to be operated from about 2 - 3 metres away.

lines.text: Squeeze the handles.

quotes.text: Squeeze the handles.

lines.text: Sweep from side to side, aiming at the base of the fire.

quotes.text: Sweep the extinguisher from side to side while aiming at the base of the fire.

lines.text: No Timer: 10-15 seconds is a range (lessons trap 1) and a countdown would pull eyes off the fire; it is shown as a fact. The PTASS steps are on FENZ's home page; the commercial page links to it ("See our advice on how to use a fire exitnguisher.").
Well done.
These FENZ pages don't say what to do once a fire is out, such as whether to stay nearby. Follow your workplace's procedure, and tell Fire and Emergency what happened when they arrive.

App wording for a gap in the sources (no aftercare: whether to stay, leave, refill or report the extinguisher). "Liaise with Fire and Emergency upon their arrival" is not quoted because in the example it follows evacuating after hours, not putting a fire out.
Stop fighting the fire. Leave now.

quotes.text: Don't put yourself or others at risk.

lines.text: Life is more important than property.

quotes.text: Remember, life is more important than property.

lines.text: Every "no" in the extinguisher check, and "still burning", comes here, then joins the main fire route at its first screen (warn others, alarm, 111), so the person who found the fire never skips raising the alarm.
Your workplace should have a Fire Action Notice. Find it and learn:

quotes.text: FIRE ACTION NOTICE

lines.text: Where the exits are.

quotes.text: EXITS ARE LOCATED

lines.text: Where the extinguishers and other firefighting equipment are.

quotes.text: FIREFIGHTING EQUIPMENT IS LOCATED

lines.text: Where to assemble.

quotes.text: ASSEMBLE

lines.text: What to do if you need help to get out.

quotes.text: IF YOU REQUIRE ASSISTANCE TO EVACUATE

lines.text: FENZ leaves these blank for each building to fill in, so this app can't tell you yours.
The FENZ notice is a form; these lines are blanks. "What to do" is app wording for the blank after "IF YOU REQUIRE ASSISTANCE TO EVACUATE".
Know a first and a second way out, and where to meet.

quotes.text: First Escape Route
Second Escape Route
Meeting Place

lines.text: Learn your workplace's evacuation scheme, so you can follow it in an emergency.

quotes.text: Your employees understand the evacuation scheme and can action it in an emergency.

lines.text: Be fast in a fire. A house fire can kill in less than three minutes.

quotes.text: Be fast
A house fire can kill you in less than three minutes.

lines.text: The advice to get low, close doors and stay out comes from FENZ's home escape plan, which FENZ also shows to businesses. FENZ lists closing doors and using extinguishers as workplace training topics, so ask about them at work.

quotes.text: Importance of closing doors to restrict fire spread
Use of fire extinguishers

lines.text: These FENZ pages say nothing about lifts. Check your workplace's plan.
"A house fire" is kept as printed rather than applied to workplaces. "Ask about them at work" is app wording.
FENZ's business checklist says a workplace should have:

quotes.text: Business fire safety checklist

lines.text: Monitored fire alarms connected to Fire and Emergency.

quotes.text: You have monitored fire alarms that are connected to the Fire and Emergency New Zealand Communication Centres.

lines.text: Fire extinguishers, and key staff trained to use them.

quotes.text: You have fire extinguishers in the building and key staff have been trained to use them.

lines.text: A working fire hose reel that emergency services can reach.

quotes.text: You have a working fire hose reel in the building that can be accessed and used by emergency services.

lines.text: An evacuation scheme approved by Fire and Emergency.

quotes.text: You have an evacuation scheme that has been approved by Fire and Emergency New Zealand.

lines.text: Shown as a list, not tick-box actions, because these are the business's to provide. No "tell your manager" advice is added (FENZ doesn't say).
There are 6 classes of fire. The right extinguisher depends on the class of fire you're most likely to have.

quotes.text: The type of fire extinguisher you need depends on the class of fire you're most likely to experience.
There are 6 classes of fire:

lines.text: A: wood, paper, plastics

quotes.text: Class A (Wood paper plastics)

lines.text: B: flammable liquids, e.g. paint, petrol, oil

quotes.text: Class B: Flammable liquids e.g. paint, petrol, oil

lines.text: C: flammable gases, e.g. LPG

quotes.text: Class C: Flammable gases e.g. butane, CNG, LPG

lines.text: D: metals, e.g. magnesium

quotes.text: Class D: Flammable metals e.g. titanium, magnesium

lines.text: E: electrical equipment

quotes.text: Class E (Electrically energised equipment)

lines.text: F: cooking oils and fats

quotes.text: Class F (Cooking oils and fats)

lines.text: Wet chemical is best for cooking oil and fat fires, but don't use it where there is live electricity.

quotes.text: A Wet Chemical extinguisher is best for extinguishing cooking oil and fat fires.
However, don't use wet chemical extinguishers on fires with a live electrical source.

lines.text: Never use dry powder on a cooking oil or fat fire: it spreads the fire.

quotes.text: you should never use it on a cooking oil or fat fire
the pressure from a dry powder extinguisher will cause the fire to spread.

lines.text: FENZ has a table of which extinguisher suits which class, but this copy of it couldn't be read. Check the label on your extinguishers, or the manufacturer's instructions.

quotes.text: For more information, refer to the manufacturer’s instructions or New Zealand Standard NZS 4503:2005

lines.text: The suitability table's marks (Recommended / Limited / Not Suitable) were unreadable, so no type-to-class pairings are given beyond what FENZ states in words.
